title: Gethsemane (Luke 22:39–46)
hook: in a garden at night he prays, sweating, not my will but yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last supper: bread, a cup, anamnesis, and remember me. After the meal, they sing, and walk out into the dark.

The night before surgery. The night before a hard goodbye. Lying awake, bargaining with the ceiling. Across the brook Cedron from Jerusalem rises the Mount of Olives, and late this night Jesus goes there, Luke says, as he often did, and his disciples follow. Matthew and Mark name the place: Gethsemane. John calls it a garden. Tradition says the name means oil press, where olives are crushed. Tonight he's the one being pressed.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DREADED THING.` → `THE MOUNT OF OLIVES, LATE.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.`

segments.voice: He tells his friends to pray that they don't fall into testing. Then he goes a stone's throw away, kneels, and prays, in the King James Bible: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Notice what he asks first: take it away. He doesn't pretend he wants to suffer; he asks, honestly, for another way. In Isaiah and Jeremiah, a cup can stand for suffering and judgment. Only then: nevertheless, the word Simon said over his empty nets. Not my will, but yours. In Mark he calls God Abba, the family word for father. Then Luke gives a detail: "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were: Luke may mean his sweat fell heavy as blood, or that it was mixed with blood; readers have taken it both ways. And a small honesty: some readers point out that these verses, with the angel who comes to strengthen him, are not in every early copy of Luke. Agony is Luke's Greek word, agonia, also used for the strain of a contest, a wrestler's or a runner's. And his friends? He comes back and finds them asleep, Luke says, sleeping for sorrow, and wakes them with a question: "Why sleep ye? rise and pray, lest ye enter into temptation." The shape of the prayer is plain: say what you want, all of it, and then, nevertheless.
screen: `REMOVE THIS CUP FROM ME.` · `NEVERTHELESS, NOT MY WILL.` · `AGONIA: A WRESTLER'S STRAIN.` · `SLEEPING FOR SORROW.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE, BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the hardest thing in front of you, something you'd take away if you could, and silently say what you really want, all of it, without dressing it up: take it away, make it different, let me off. Then, if you can, notice what it would be like to hold it a little more loosely; you don't have to get to nevertheless today. If you pray, you can pray it to God just as honestly.
Gethsemane. A garden whose name, tradition says, means oil press, where he prayed take this cup away, and then, not my will.
Your line: not my will. He asked honestly first, then said nevertheless. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many churches keep a watch on the night of Maundy Thursday, staying up to pray in memory of Gethsemane, and some Christians keep a holy hour of prayer on other nights. Pilgrims to Jerusalem visit an olive garden on the Mount of Olives with very old trees.

chat.says: In Gethsemane, did Jesus pretend he wasn't afraid?
options: No. He honestly asked for the cup to be taken away, then said not my will.
Yes. He only prayed that God's will be done and asked for nothing else.
No. He was afraid, so he asked his friends to pray in his place instead.
chat.meaning: He asked first: remove this cup. He didn't pretend to want to suffer. Only then: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.

notes: Luke 22:43–44 is absent from several early manuscripts (e.g., P75, Codex Vaticanus) and present in others (e.g., Codex Sinaiticus original hand, Bezae); stated plainly and neutrally.
The script does not claim hematidrosis; it gives both readings of 'as it were'.
'They sing' in the review: Mark 14:26 / Matthew 26:30 ('when they had sung an hymn').

The practice invites honest, unscripted prayer in the listener's own words; no prayer text is written. The index practice reads 'pray the hardest honest prayer you have'; phrased as an invitation for those who pray.
Maundy Thursday watch (altar of repose) and holy hour in howItsDone; confirm.
